sections.h2: Who sends the tax bill in Cole County, and who sets the value?
sections.html:
The Assessor decides what a parcel is worth for tax purposes. The Collector of Revenue, in Room 100 of the Courthouse Annex at 311 E High Street, Jefferson City 65101, mails the bills and takes the money. The Collector answers at 573-634-9124 on weekdays from 8 in the morning until 4:30 in the afternoon, and a 24 hour drop box waits outside the Annex entrance that faces High Street.

The Assessor's page counts over 33,000 real estate parcels and more than 30,000 personal property accounts in Cole County. Collections run past 94 million dollars a year, divided among the state, several municipalities, rural fire districts, the public library and the school districts. The County Clerk keeps the hearing calendar for the Board of Equalization.

Above the county sits the Missouri State Tax Commission, which supervises assessors and takes appeals after the local board has ruled. Send value questions to the Assessor and bill questions to the Collector.

sections.h2: What are the payment deadlines and late costs on a Cole County bill?
sections.html:
A real estate bill falls due as soon as you receive it and in any case by December 31. For mail, the postmark counts. Bills go out during November, and the Collector says to phone if yours has not shown up by the second week of December, since an unreceived bill still carries the tax and any late fees.

  • Charges for the first year of delinquency can climb as high as 25%.
  • Unpaid tax is a lien that follows the real estate, so whoever buys the property takes on what is owed.
  • If the bill belongs to your lender's escrow account, pass it along to the lender.
  • Sellers who still receive a bill for a house they sold should give the Collector the buyer's name and address.

The online system takes cards with a 2.25% convenience fee and echecks with a $1.75 fee (plan on 5 to 7 days to clear). You can also call 855-568-0066, walk in, or mail a check. Mail bearing a December 31 postmark is on time, and the drop box stays open until midnight that night. At the counter the office takes cash, personal check, cashier's check, bank draft, money order or card, and one check may cover several bills.

sections.h2: How is the Cole County tax amount worked out?
sections.html:
Divide the assessed value by 100, then multiply by the levy. The Collector's worked example takes $9,500 of assessed value at $5.1240 and arrives at $486.78. Assessed value is a fraction of market value, and the fraction depends on how the parcel is classified.

Class of real estateShare of value assessed
Residential19%

Commercial32%

Picture a $200,000 home: at 19%, the assessed figure is $38,000, and the levy is charged against each hundred of that. Voters and the taxing districts set the levies, and the Assessor's page links a rate sheet. Ask which taxing districts cover your parcel before you estimate a bill.

sections.h2: How do I challenge a Cole County valuation?
sections.html:
An informal conversation with the Assessor comes first. It is voluntary and available on weekdays during office hours. Show proof of market value: photographs, an inspection report, a recent appraisal or nearby sales. The county reminds owners that the Assessor's role is to keep values in line with the current market.

Formal review happens at the Board of Equalization, and RSMo 137.275 puts the filing deadline on the second Monday in July. Cole County seats its three Commissioners, a non-voting Assessor, two appointees who hold no county office and, for parcels inside Jefferson City, two city appointees. The County Clerk records the proceedings and mails each taxpayer the written decision.

A remaining dispute can go to the State Tax Commission. RSMo 138.430 allows the appeal within the period stated in that chapter or 30 days after the local board finishes, whichever ends later. Cole County describes these sessions as typically held in September and October, before one Administrative Hearing Officer, with an appraisal expected and a lawyer optional.

sections.h2: When does Cole County sell land for unpaid tax?
sections.html:
Parcels delinquent for three years are eligible for the county's certificate sale. It starts at 10 in the morning on the fourth Monday of August at the Cole County Courthouse, a date that RSMo 140.150 applies across Missouri. Paying the tax, penalty, interest and costs to the Collector ahead of the sale stops it for that parcel.

  • The News Tribune in Jefferson City runs the parcel list for three consecutive weeks beforehand.
  • Whoever wins the bid holds a certificate of purchase, and the owner has a year from the sale to redeem.
  • Liens on the property survive the sale and the redemption window.
  • A winning bidder who fails to pay risks a 25% penalty plus a prosecuting attorney fee.

An owner who is behind and weighing a sale can ask the Collector for the current payoff. The Collector's page says no tax is paid to that office at the moment of a sale, so request any payoff figure in writing through your title company.

sections.h2: Who covers the year's tax when a Cole County house changes hands?
sections.html:
Whoever owns the house in the fall pays the November bill, and that is the buyer. The Collector's page says taxes are generally prorated, so the buyer is credited at closing for the days or months the seller held the property. The buyer then pays the entire bill by December 31.

The county sits in central Missouri below the Missouri River and spans 402 square miles. Jefferson City serves as seat and state capital. William Temple Cole gave the county its name when it was organized on November 16, 1820. It borders Boone, Callaway, Osage, Miller and Moniteau counties, and US 50, 54 and 63 plus Routes 17 and 179 cross it.

Census estimates for July 1, 2025 show 77,908 people and 33,956 homes and other housing units. About 67.9% of units are owner-occupied, the 2020 to 2024 median value is $229,600 and household income has a median of $74,876. Rent has a median of $834, workers travel 17.9 minutes on average, and 154 building permits were issued in 2025.

Public school districts reaching into the county are Jefferson City Public Schools, Blair Oaks R-II, Cole County R-I at Russellville, Cole County R-V at Eugene and Jamestown C-1. Incorporated places include Jefferson City, Lohman, Russellville, St. Martins, St. Thomas, Taos, Centertown and Wardsville.

faqs.q: What day does Cole County property tax become late?
faqs.a: After December 31. The bill is payable on receipt, mailed payments are judged by postmark and the courthouse drop box stays open until midnight that night. Charges during the first delinquent year can run up to 25%.

faqs.q: Can I count on the Collector mailing my bill?
faqs.a: Bills are mailed in November. If none has come by the second week of December, phone 573-634-9124. The obligation and late fees stand even when a bill is lost.

faqs.q: Until what date can a Cole County owner appeal to the Board of Equalization?
faqs.a: The second Monday in July, with the filing made through the County Clerk. An informal meeting with the Assessor can come earlier.

faqs.q: Do the buyer or the seller owe the property tax after a mid-year Cole County sale?
faqs.a: The buyer owes the whole bill due in December. Proration between the parties normally gives the buyer a credit at closing, and nothing is paid to the Collector during closing. A seller who still gets the bill should send the Collector the buyer's address.

faqs.q: How many years of unpaid tax lead to a Cole County sale?
faqs.a: Three. After that the parcel can be offered at the August certificate sale, and the owner may still pay what is due before the sale or redeem within a year after it.
